paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across tasks to improve learning on a new task. This paper asks how the distribution of those tasks determines the error that remains possible. It studies a specific mathematical setting: linear regression with fixed inputs, Gaussian observation noise, and a Gaussian distribution over task parameters. Within this setting, it establishes lower bounds on transfer risk that apply to any algorithm.

The authors also develop a weighted version of biased regularized regression that matches those bounds within a fixed constant factor. Its weights come from the covariance of the task distribution, which describes how task parameters vary together. This connects the best achievable performance to the structure of variation across tasks.

The framework brings parameter sharing and representation learning into the same analysis. Representation learning appears when the task covariance is unknown. For that case, the authors propose an expectation-maximization method with efficient updates. Their experiments show that it can approach the lower bound as more tasks become available and compete successfully with alternatives for representation learning.
icml-2021-a-distribution-dependent-analy.tldr: In a Gaussian linear-regression setting, task covariance determines meta-learning difficulty and guides a method that matches theoretical lower bounds within a constant factor.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function that makes a desired policy optimal in a given decision-making environment. This paper studies how much data that inference can require when the environment has finitely many states and actions. Its contribution is an information-theoretic lower bound, describing a fundamental obstacle to learning rather than proposing a faster reward-learning algorithm.

The argument constructs a collection of reward-inference problems using spherical codes, a geometric way of arranging separated possibilities. The constructed problems satisfy a specified strict-separation condition. The authors analyze both the size of this collection and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the trajectories it generates. These quantities capture how many alternatives must be distinguished and how informative the observations are for distinguishing them.

Combining this construction with Fano’s inequality yields the sample-complexity lower bound reported in the abstract as O(n log n), where n is the number of states. The finding links the difficulty of reward inference to environment size through the information available in trajectories, rather than through the computational design of a particular algorithm.
icml-2021-a-lower-bound-for-the-sample-c.tldr: The paper derives an information-theoretic lower bound, reported as O(n log n), for finite-state inverse reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: When several reinforcement-learning agents share an environment, each agent faces a moving target: the others change their behavior while learning. An agent’s own learning also changes the experiences it encounters. The paper addresses both sources of change, treating adaptation as part of the learning problem rather than assuming that interaction partners maintain fixed policies.

Its central contribution is a meta-multiagent policy-gradient theorem. The resulting gradient updates account for how the agent’s own policy evolves and how other agents’ policies evolve. This provides a theoretical basis for learning how to adapt within an environment whose behavior keeps changing. The authors present the framework as a general treatment that incorporates key aspects of previous leading approaches.

The method is tested across multiagent benchmarks involving cooperation, competition, and mixed incentives. In these evaluations, it adapts more efficiently to new agents as those agents learn than the baseline methods. The findings support explicitly modeling learning dynamics on both sides of an interaction when designing adaptable multiagent behavior.
icml-2021-a-policy-gradient-algorithm-fo.tldr: A policy-gradient framework models both an agent’s learning and other agents’ learning, improving adaptation efficiency across diverse multiagent benchmarks.

paragraphs: Model evaluation needs labeled examples, and obtaining those labels can be as expensive as labeling training data. This paper introduces active testing to reduce that cost. Instead of treating a large labeled test set as freely available, it selects which test examples to label so that a model’s performance can be estimated with fewer labels.

The selection rules are designed specifically for evaluation. An example that helps train a model is not necessarily the example that most improves an estimate of its performance. The authors derive acquisition strategies around this distinction. They also address a statistical problem created by selective labeling: choosing examples nonuniformly can bias the evaluation. Their approach removes that bias while also reducing the estimator’s variance.

Active testing is presented as straightforward to implement and applicable to any supervised learning method. Experiments include WideResNets and Gaussian processes, with datasets including Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-100. The stated results demonstrate its effectiveness, supporting selective test labeling as a way to make evaluation more economical without simply accepting a biased performance estimate.
icml-2021-active-testing-sample-efficien.tldr: Active testing selects informative test examples and corrects selection bias to estimate model performance using fewer labels.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good choices using observations of an unknown objective. This paper considers settings where those observations can be adversarially biased, including bias caused by an uncontrolled hidden confounder. The challenge is that an observed outcome can reflect both the choice being evaluated and an outside influence, complicating the search for the best choice.

The authors first reduce this confounded optimization problem to a dueling-bandit problem, which frames learning around comparisons between alternatives. They then introduce a dueling-bandit approach based on information-directed sampling. The resulting method uses kernels to handle nonlinear reward structure and comes with guarantees on cumulative regret, a measure of the performance lost while learning.

The paper presents this as the first efficient kernelized dueling-bandit algorithm with such guarantees. Its analysis also extends an earlier semiparametric linear-bandit model to nonlinear rewards and identifies connections to doubly robust estimation. Together, these contributions provide a theoretical route from optimization with biased observations to comparison-based learning with controlled cumulative loss.
icml-2021-bias-robust-bayesian-optimizat.tldr: The paper converts Bayesian optimization with adversarially biased observations into a kernelized dueling-bandit problem with cumulative-regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Small convolutional networks specialized for particular vision tasks can leave much of a datacenter accelerator’s capacity unused. Their low arithmetic intensity means their workload does not make effective use of the available computation. Increasing batch size helps, but the authors identify diminishing returns: even large batches can leave these specialized networks using accelerators poorly.

FoldedCNNs changes the network’s input and layer structure to address this problem. It combines f images, each with C channels, into one input with fC channels. A wider convolutional network then classifies those images jointly. This changes how computation is organized inside the model, raising arithmetic intensity beyond what increasing the ordinary batch size achieves.

The reported evaluations show throughput improvements of up to 2.5 times and GPU-utilization improvements of up to 2.8 times. Accuracy remains close to that of the original network in most cases. These qualified results suggest that redesigning specialized networks around accelerator use can improve inference efficiency, while making accuracy preservation an empirical consideration rather than an automatic guarantee.
icml-2021-boosting-the-throughput-and-ac.tldr: FoldedCNNs jointly processes images through a wider network, improving throughput and GPU utilization while retaining similar accuracy in most tested cases.

paragraphs: Healthcare produces large amounts of physiological data without labels. CLOCS explores how cardiac signals can provide useful training information before labels are available. It uses contrastive learning, which trains representations by encouraging selected instances to have similar internal descriptions. The goal is to make unlabeled recordings contribute to models that will later perform supervised tasks.

The proposed family of methods organizes this similarity learning across spatial, temporal, and patient dimensions. That choice makes the structure of cardiac data central to pretraining. The authors assess the resulting representations through both linear evaluation and fine-tuning on downstream tasks, testing their usefulness in two different ways of adapting pretrained features.

Across the reported evaluations, CLOCS consistently outperforms BYOL and SimCLR. It also shows strong generalization with only 25% of the labeled training data. In addition, its training procedure produces patient-specific representations that can quantify similarity between patients. The findings therefore concern both reduced dependence on labels and the creation of representations that describe relationships among patients.
icml-2021-clocs-contrastive-learning-of-.tldr: CLOCS learns cardiac-signal representations from unlabeled data, outperforming BYOL and SimCLR in reported downstream evaluations and supporting patient-similarity measurement.

paragraphs: A written sentence can be spoken with different pitches and rhythms, so text-to-speech must model more than a single fixed audio output. This paper introduces a parallel, end-to-end speech-generation method that explicitly represents that variability. It addresses a quality gap identified between earlier single-stage systems and systems that generate speech in two stages.

The method combines variational inference, normalizing flows, and adversarial training to increase the expressive power of its generative model. A stochastic duration predictor adds variation in timing, allowing the same text to produce different rhythms. Together, uncertainty in the latent variables and variability in duration capture multiple plausible ways of speaking an input.

Human listeners evaluate the generated speech using mean opinion scores on LJ Speech, a single-speaker dataset. In that evaluation, the method outperforms the best publicly available text-to-speech systems and receives scores comparable to ground-truth audio. This supports the quality of the proposed combination in the tested setting; the comparison concerns listener ratings on that dataset.
icml-2021-conditional-variational-autoen.tldr: A parallel end-to-end speech model captures variable pitch and rhythm and achieves human quality ratings comparable to ground-truth audio on LJ Speech.

paragraphs: Decentralized training distributes learning across connected devices, supporting both on-device learning and large compute clusters. However, the resulting models can perform worse than models trained centrally. The paper studies this gap through consensus distance: how far the devices’ models diverge from one another as training proceeds. This offers a common quantity for examining effects associated with network size, communication structure, and data partitioning.

The theoretical result is conditional. When the training consensus distance stays below a critical quantity, decentralized training converges as quickly as its centralized counterpart. The claim therefore identifies a sufficient level of agreement for matching convergence speed, rather than saying that every decentralized training configuration has equivalent behavior.

Experiments show that the relationship between consensus distance and generalization performance is consistent with the theoretical observation. The authors use these findings to develop practical training guidelines and demonstrate their effectiveness in a datacenter setting. The contribution turns disagreement among devices into a quantity that can guide training design and help mitigate the observed performance drop.
icml-2021-consensus-control-for-decentra.tldr: Controlling disagreement between devices can help decentralized training match centralized convergence speed under a stated consensus-distance condition.

paragraphs: A classifier’s uncertainty estimate is useful only if it remains informative when the model encounters difficult or manipulated inputs. Dirichlet-based uncertainty models predict the parameters of a probability distribution alongside class predictions, providing fast uncertainty estimates. This paper examines whether those estimates remain reliable under adversarial attacks through a large-scale, detailed robustness study.

The evaluation separates three uses of uncertainty: identifying correct versus incorrect predictions, detecting adversarial examples, and distinguishing data from the training distribution from out-of-distribution data. The results suggest that the evaluated models’ uncertainty estimates are not robust for these tasks. This matters because an uncertainty output can fail in ways that are distinct from a wrong class prediction.

The authors also investigate ways to improve robustness. Adversarial training has only a minor effect in their study, whereas their median-smoothing approach produces a significant improvement. The findings therefore both challenge the reliability of the tested uncertainty estimates under attack and identify a promising mitigation, without establishing that smoothing makes every uncertainty judgment reliable.
icml-2021-evaluating-robustness-of-predi.tldr: Adversarial evaluations expose weaknesses in Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimates, while a median-smoothing approach substantially improves their robustness.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents may encounter environments that were unavailable during training. This paper asks how to give meaningful safety assurances for that situation. It considers a collection of Markov decision processes available for training and new processes sampled from the same underlying distribution. A new environment can therefore differ from every training environment while still belonging to the distribution covered by the analysis.

The authors present several classes of algorithms with probabilistic guarantees of safe generalization. Safety is not restricted to one fixed definition: the work considers multiple definitions and allows users to specify the safety requirements of interest. The guarantees concern satisfying those requirements when transferring to environments sampled in the stated way.

These methods belong to the Seldonian family of learning algorithms, which return models with probabilistic safety assurances. The contribution connects that approach to reinforcement learning across environments. Its scope depends on both the chosen safety definition and the shared-distribution assumption; it does not turn safety on unseen environments into an unconditional or certain property.
icml-2021-high-confidence-generalization.tldr: The paper develops reinforcement-learning algorithms with probabilistic safety guarantees for unseen environments sampled from the same distribution as training environments.

paragraphs: Transformer language models can require substantial memory, inference time, and power. Quantization reduces numerical precision, but earlier Transformer quantization approaches still use floating-point calculations during inference. I-BERT addresses this remaining dependency so that the entire inference process can use integer arithmetic, making the computation better suited to hardware with integer-only execution units.

The key technical step is handling nonlinear operations that would otherwise require floating point. I-BERT provides lightweight integer approximations for operations including GELU, Softmax, and Layer Normalization. Combining these with quantization produces end-to-end integer-only BERT inference, rather than leaving selected operations outside the integer computation path.

On GLUE tasks using RoBERTa-Base and RoBERTa-Large, the method achieves accuracy similar to, and slightly above, the full-precision baseline. A preliminary implementation reports INT8 inference speedups of 2.4 to 4.0 times over FP32 on a T4 GPU system. These results demonstrate the approach’s practical potential on the evaluated models and hardware, with the speed measurements explicitly tied to that preliminary implementation.
icml-2021-i-bert-integer-only-bert-quant.tldr: I-BERT enables fully integer Transformer inference, retaining comparable GLUE accuracy and reporting preliminary T4 GPU speedups of 2.4–4.0 times.

paragraphs: Neural recordings reveal spikes, but understanding population activity also requires identifying the hidden processes that generate them. This paper introduces Poisson Latent Neural Differential Equations, or PLNDE, to infer those processes. The model describes a low-dimensional nonlinear hidden state with neural ordinary differential equations, accepts noisy sensory inputs, and produces Poisson spike-train outputs.

On synthetic datasets, PLNDE accurately recovers phase portraits and fixed points: descriptions of how hidden states move and where their dynamics settle. The tested systems include an oscillator, a three-dimensional nonlinear spiral, and a sensory decision-making model with attractors. These evaluations assess whether the model recovers dynamical structure as well as activity over time.

The authors report substantially better inference of single-trial firing rates and latent trajectories than existing methods, especially with few spikes and few trials. They also apply PLNDE to recordings across regions of rat medial frontal cortex during an auditory decision task. The framework offers an interpretable way to investigate neural computation through the dynamics underlying observed spikes.
icml-2021-inferring-latent-dynamics-unde.tldr: PLNDE uses neural differential equations to recover hidden neural dynamics from spike trains, with strong reported performance when spikes and trials are scarce.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to approximate a target probability distribution when its density is known only up to a normalization constant. It starts from Kernel Stein Discrepancy, a measure of difference between distributions, and investigates the associated Wasserstein gradient flow. This turns the problem of matching a distribution into a process for moving an approximation toward the target.

The resulting algorithm, KSD Descent, represents the target with a collection of particles and moves them deterministically using score information. A central practical feature is its tractable loss function. That explicit objective allows the use of robust optimization schemes such as L-BFGS, an advantage the authors contrast with other particle methods, including Stein Variational Gradient Descent.

The paper examines convergence properties and demonstrates practical relevance, but also establishes concrete failure cases. KSD Descent can become trapped in spurious local minima, so optimizing its loss does not invariably produce the desired distribution. The contribution therefore combines an implementable sampling approach with an analysis of both its useful optimization structure and its possible failure behavior.
icml-2021-kernel-stein-discrepancy-desce.tldr: KSD Descent approximates distributions with deterministically optimized particles and a tractable loss, but can get stuck in spurious local minima.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces labeling work by asking for labels on selected examples. In streaming settings, however, storage or privacy constraints can prevent retaining data indefinitely. A model must decide what to query and how to update as examples arrive. This makes it difficult to choose representative examples while learning efficiently without forgetting earlier information.

Message Passing Adaptive Resonance Theory, or MPART, learns the distribution and connectivity structure of incoming data online. It represents that structure with a topological graph and passes information through the graph to guide label requests. The selection process seeks examples that are both informative and representative, while classification learning uses labeled and unlabeled data.

The authors evaluate MPART in stream-based selective-sampling settings using comparable query-selection strategies. They report that it significantly outperforms competitive models in those evaluations. The approach matters because it links immediate labeling decisions to an evolving picture of the data’s structure, allowing unlabeled observations to support continued learning as the stream arrives.
icml-2021-message-passing-adaptive-reson.tldr: MPART uses an evolving data graph and message passing to select labels and learn from streams, outperforming competitive models in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: NeRF-VAE combines a generative model of scenes with an explicit three-dimensional rendering process. It uses neural radiance fields and differentiable volume rendering to incorporate geometric structure. Unlike fitting a separate NeRF for each scene, the model learns shared structure across scenes and uses amortized inference to infer a new scene without retraining.

The model is a variational autoencoder whose latent scene representation conditions a radiance field. Learning a distribution over those fields connects variation between scenes with the geometry used to render their images. This is a central distinction from the convolution-based rendering models discussed in the paper, which lack an explicit geometric rendering structure.

On previously unseen synthetic environments, the trained model infers and renders geometrically consistent scenes from very few input images. It also generalizes well to out-of-distribution cameras in the reported comparisons, where convolutional models do not. An additional attention-based mechanism for conditioning the decoder improves performance. The findings support combining shared scene learning with explicit geometry for inference across scenes and camera configurations.
icml-2021-nerf-vae-a-geometry-aware-3d-s.tldr: NeRF-VAE learns shared scene structure to infer new synthetic 3D scenes without retraining and render them consistently across camera views.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from previously collected experience. Many approaches encourage the learned policy to stay close to the behavior represented in that data by adding a policy-divergence penalty. This paper develops an alternative that builds information about the data-generating behavior directly into the critic, the component that evaluates state-action choices.

The critic is expressed as the logarithm of the behavior policy plus a learnable state-action value offset. A neural network can learn that offset, and behavior regularization becomes a suitable constraint on this component. The authors propose a gradient penalty and show that it is equivalent to Fisher-divergence regularization, connecting the construction to score matching and energy-based generative models.

The resulting algorithm is Fisher-BRC, short for Behavior Regularized Critic. On standard offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks, it achieves better performance and faster convergence than existing leading methods. The contribution offers a different location and mathematical form for behavior regularization: shaping the critic’s learned adjustment to the behavior policy.
icml-2021-offline-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Fisher-BRC regularizes a behavior-informed critic through a gradient penalty, improving performance and convergence on standard offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex-concave saddle problems, where one variable is minimized while another is maximized. The variables interact through a linear operator. The minimizing side includes a smooth convex function restricted to a bounded convex polytope, while the maximizing side can involve a nonsmooth convex function. Such formulations arise in relaxations of discrete optimization problems.

The approach assumes two efficient computational tools: a linear minimization oracle for the polytope-constrained side and a proximal map for the other side. It combines Frank-Wolfe updates with proximal primal-dual algorithms to exploit that asymmetric structure. In the general setting, the authors prove an O(1/n) primal-dual gap using O(n log n) oracle calls.

Stronger results hold in specified special cases. With a quadratic smooth function and an indicator of a linear constraint, the dual objective converges at O(1/n²). For the stated equality-constrained formulation, the primal and infeasibility gaps also have O(1/n²) bounds. The authors present these as improvements over known rates for the considered class and show applications to labeling problems.
icml-2021-one-sided-frank-wolfe-algorith.tldr: Combining Frank-Wolfe and proximal updates yields convergence guarantees for structured saddle problems, with faster rates under specified quadratic and constraint conditions.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows offer efficient likelihood evaluation, but good samples often require deep models that are difficult to train. Another issue is poor conditioning: an invertible transformation can have a Jacobian close to singular when representing data concentrated near lower-dimensional structure. This paper studies how depth and conditioning affect what flow models can represent.

For affine coupling architectures, the authors prove that a constant number of layers can exactly represent a permutation or a 1 × 1 convolution. Thus, the choice of partition is not itself a representational bottleneck for depth in that sense. They also prove that shallow affine coupling networks can approximate distributions universally in Wasserstein distance if ill-conditioning is permitted.

That qualification connects expressive power to potentially difficult numerical behavior. The paper additionally investigates padding experimentally and proves a depth lower bound for general flow architectures with few neurons per layer and bounded Lipschitz constant. Together, the results distinguish what shallow models can represent when conditioning is unrestricted from what constrained architectures may require in depth.
icml-2021-representational-aspects-of-de.tldr: The paper characterizes how flow depth and conditioning interact, including shallow universality when ill-conditioning is allowed and depth lower bounds under constraints.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards from decision-making behavior. This paper asks a more basic question: whether the reward can be identified within the chosen model at all. That question matters when a Markov decision process is used to explain a real decision maker or to reason about how their behavior might change under different circumstances.

The authors formalize reward identification and study how it depends on properties of the decision-process model. Their central result concerns deterministic Markov decision processes with a maximum-entropy reinforcement-learning objective. For that setting, they prove necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiability, specifying exactly when the relevant identification property holds.

They then use those conditions to construct efficient algorithms that test whether a model is identifiable. This provides a way to examine the model’s suitability for reward inference before interpreting an inferred reward as an explanation of behavior. The theoretical characterization is tied to the deterministic, maximum-entropy setting stated in the paper.
icml-2021-reward-identification-in-inver.tldr: The paper gives necessary and sufficient reward-identifiability conditions, plus efficient tests, for deterministic decision processes with a maximum-entropy learning objective.

paragraphs: Entropy-regularized optimal transport is commonly computed with Sinkhorn iterations, but constructing the full matrix of pairwise costs makes the standard approach quadratic in problem size. This paper replaces that costly matrix with approximations that support log-linear computation, targeting large collections of objects in the high-dimensional spaces used by deep learning.

The first approximation is sparse and uses locality-sensitive hashing. The second combines a Nyström approximation with sparse corrections based on that hashing scheme; the authors call it locally corrected Nyström. They analyze these constructions theoretically and evaluate them both as transport approximations and as components of larger applications.

For unsupervised word-embedding alignment, the approximations make an existing leading method three times faster and improve accuracy by 3.1 percentage points without other model changes. For graph-distance regression, the proposed graph transport network combines graph neural networks with the enhanced Sinkhorn computation. The authors report a 48% improvement over previous models while retaining log-linear scaling in node count. These application results show that the computational savings can accompany stronger task performance.
icml-2021-scalable-optimal-transport-in-.tldr: Two cost-matrix approximations enable log-linear entropy-regularized optimal transport and improve reported word-alignment and graph-distance results.

paragraphs: A Lipschitz constant bounds how strongly a function’s output can change relative to its input. Such bounds matter in work on robustness, generative-model training, distribution distances, and invertible networks. This paper brings that analysis to self-attention, whose interactions between sequence elements differ from the linear maps and pointwise nonlinearities studied in many earlier network bounds.

The authors prove that standard dot-product self-attention is not Lipschitz on an unbounded input domain. The domain qualification is part of the result: it concerns a global bound when input size is unrestricted. They propose L2 self-attention as an alternative that is Lipschitz and derive an upper bound on its Lipschitz constant.

Experiments provide evidence that the bound is asymptotically tight, supporting its accuracy in the regime studied rather than establishing tightness purely by proof. To demonstrate practical relevance, the authors construct invertible self-attention and use it in a Transformer for character-level language modeling. The work connects attention’s mathematical sensitivity to the design of architectures requiring controlled transformations.
icml-2021-the-lipschitz-constant-of-self.tldr: Standard dot-product attention is not Lipschitz on unbounded inputs; the paper introduces a bounded-sensitivity L2 alternative and demonstrates invertible self-attention.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery asks an agent to acquire useful behaviors without external rewards or supervision. The challenge is to discover a varied set of behaviors and organize them into meaningful skills. This paper introduces Information Bottleneck Option Learning, or IBOL, which combines a mechanism for encouraging varied transitions with an abstraction method for the skills that emerge.

The approach builds on environment linearization that promotes transitions to more varied and more distant states. It then uses the information-bottleneck framework to abstract learned skills into options. The authors describe this abstraction as improving stability and encouraging disentanglement, so the method addresses both the diversity of discovered behavior and how that behavior is represented.

The evaluation compares IBOL with multiple leading unsupervised skill-discovery methods in MuJoCo environments, including Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, and D’Kitty. IBOL performs better on the reported information-theoretic evaluations and downstream tasks. These results support the combination of broader transition discovery and bottleneck-based skill abstraction in the tested environments.
icml-2021-unsupervised-skill-discovery-w.tldr: IBOL combines diverse state transitions with information-bottleneck skill abstraction, outperforming compared skill-discovery methods on reported MuJoCo evaluations.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language models often begin with an expensive image-processing stage before combining visual and textual information. The authors identify two problems with this design: extracting visual features can cost far more computation than the multimodal interaction itself, and the visual embedder’s predefined vocabulary can restrict what the overall model expresses.

ViLT simplifies that visual front end. It processes visual inputs in a convolution-free manner analogous to textual inputs, producing a minimal, unified vision-and-language Transformer without region supervision. The architectural change directly targets the feature-extraction stage that the paper identifies as a major source of computational cost and representational restriction.

The reported results show speed improvements of up to tens of times over previous vision-and-language pretraining models, alongside competitive or better downstream performance. The speed statement is an upper-end result, rather than a fixed multiplier for every task. The findings show that substantial simplification of visual input processing can coexist with strong joint vision-and-language performance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2021-vilt-vision-and-language-trans.tldr: ViLT simplifies visual input processing to deliver speedups of up to tens of times while retaining competitive or better vision-and-language task performance.

paragraphs: A model can lose accuracy when the data it encounters differs from its training data. WILDS addresses the limited representation of these real-world distribution shifts in commonly used benchmarks. It brings together ten datasets covering naturally occurring changes, including differences between hospitals, wildlife camera locations, and the times and places represented in satellite imagery and poverty mapping.

The authors evaluate standard training on each dataset and find substantially worse performance outside the training distribution than within it. Existing methods designed to address distribution shift also leave a performance gap. These findings establish that the benchmark captures challenges that the evaluated training approaches do not resolve.

WILDS also provides an open-source package with automated dataset loading, default architectures and hyperparameters, and standardized evaluations. This infrastructure makes the collection usable for developing and comparing new methods. The contribution combines evidence of persistent generalization problems with a shared testing framework grounded in shifts that arise in practical applications.
icml-2021-wilds-a-benchmark-of-in-the-wi.tldr: WILDS provides ten datasets of real-world distribution shifts and shows persistent performance gaps for standard training and evaluated shift-handling methods.
